raw_segments.text: Look, old man, you see, blind of one eye and the left ear is torn, just the marks you described
to me.
It was by that I found him, I found him directly.
He did not belong to anyone," he explained, turning quickly to the captain, to his wife,
to Alyosha, and then again to Alyosha.
He used to live in the Fedetov's backyard.
Though he made his home there, they did not feed him.
He was a stray dog that had run away from the village.
I found him.
You see, old man, he couldn't have swallowed what you gave him.
If he had, he must have died, he must have, so he must have spat it out since he is alive.
You did not see him do it.
But the pin pricked his tongue, that is why he squealed.
He ran away squealing and you thought he'd swallowed it.
He might well squeal because the skin of dogs' mouths is so tender, tenderer than in men
much tenderer," Kalia cried impetuously, his face glowing and radiant with delight.
Alyosha could not speak.
White as a sheet, he gazed open-mouthed at Kalia, with his great eyes almost starting
out of his head.
And if Krasetkin, who had no suspicion of it, had known what a disastrous and fatal
effect such a moment might have on the sick child's health, nothing would have induced
him to play such a trick on him.
But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who realized it.
As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
